1.pericope_label: Joseph visits his dying father; Ephraim and Manasseh adopted; Rachel remembered
debates: Why Rachel is named at this point: Ellicott makes it the justification of the act, since Jacob grounds the double portion not on her rank as chief wife but on the untimely death that prevented her bearing more sons; Calvin makes it a spur, that the name of Joseph’s mother should move him, since she left her father and journeyed into a distant land at God’s command and her example ought to induce her sons to bid farewell to Egypt; Clarke makes it pure affection, that many waters cannot quench love; Wesley makes it grief, that strong affections in the enjoyment cause long afflictions in the loss

On what ground the double portion rests: Keil states the legal ground, that the promise of increase and of Canaan empowered the patriarch to adopt sons born in Egypt and outside the range of his house; Ellicott works out the consequence, that Ephraim is reckoned firstborn and Manasseh second, the firstborn’s legal right being a double share, while the birthright in the spiritual sense was Judah’s, Reuben being excluded for his sin and Simeon and Levi for their cruelty; Calvin will not let the transaction pass without wonder that a dying exile assigns a sixth part of a land he does not possess

Whether Joseph had sons after Ephraim and Manasseh: Ellicott thinks probably not and holds that any such would have ranked only as heads of families under their brothers, while Gill reports Jarchi’s conditional reading, that the clause supposes rather than asserts
outliers: Ellicott's account of what the chapter is for, that the earlier genealogy recognised heads of families whereas here Jacob bestows two tribes, an act no authority less than his would have sufficed for
Calvin's contrast between a private man's last will and the method of one with whom God had established a covenant
Henry's pastoral notes on the visit, that a sick bed is a proper place both for giving counsel and receiving instruction, and that Manasseh and Ephraim would never forget what passed that day
Clarke's use of this verse to settle a difficulty in the preceding chapter, that Jacob's sitting upon the bed proves a bed and not a staff was meant there

Ellicott's aside on the name Luz, that it shows how slowly new titles displaced native ones, compared with the recent exploration of Palestine where Seleucid and Roman names were never adopted by the peasantry
Calvin's proverb against the transaction and his answer to it, that no one can give what he has not, and yet from this it appears with what firm faith the fathers relied upon the word of the Lord
themes: the adoption of Ephraim and Manasseh

8.pericope_label: Who are these; bring them unto me; Joseph bows with his face to the earth
debates: Whether the question about the young men is a real one: Gill and Clarke read it at face value from the blindness, that Jacob could see two figures but not distinguish them until they were brought near; Ellicott takes it as a formal turn rather than a failure of sight, the solemn addressing of the discourse to those about to be invested with patriarchal rank; Calvin doubts the sequence altogether, having no doubt that Jacob had inquired about the youths before naming them his heirs, and holding that the narrative has placed the question after the event it preceded

Who performed the act of reverence: Ellicott reports that the Samaritan, the Syriac and the Septuagint treat the Hebrew verb as a contracted plural, which many moderns follow and which would make Manasseh and Ephraim the ones who bowed with their faces toward the ground, but judges that the pronoun favours the singular and that the sense is equally satisfactory either way

What Joseph’s prostration proves: Delaney, quoted by Clarke, extolled it as a condescension the more admirable because the father was poor and blind and decrepit; Clarke calls this insufferable, holding that it says in effect that a young man raised to affluence performs a wonder in showing respect to his father, and that the maxim underneath it is that children who have risen to affluence are not obliged to reverence parents who have been reduced
outliers: Henry's conclusion from the blindness, that the eye of faith may be very clear even when the eye of the body is very much clouded
Henry's notice of what the apostle does with this scene, singling out this blessing for mention while passing over the blessing of the rest of the sons, though that too was done in faith
Calvin's account of why offspring degenerates, that few heartily acknowledge their seed to be given them, and the ingratitude of the world cannot perceive the effect of God's blessings
Gill's support for the sentiment from a heathen quarter, that the Greeks and Romans formed Theodorus and Deodatus and Apollodorus and Artemidorus on the same principle as Mattaniah and Nathaniel

Keil's reconstruction of the positions, that Joseph came up with Ephraim the younger at his own right hand and Manasseh the elder at his left, so that Ephraim stood at Jacob's right hand and Manasseh at his left
Calvin's distinction that the imposition of hands looked higher than the division of the land, to their becoming two of the patriarchs of the Church
themes: the eyes of Israel were dim
I had not thought to see thy face
bowed with his face to the earth

13.pericope_label: Israel crosses his hands; the God who fed me, the Angel which redeemed me
debates: What the words describing the act mean: Ellicott reports that the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Vulgate render them placing his hands crosswise while the Targum of Onkelos supports the received rendering, guiding his hands wittingly, and allows some philological support for the three chief versions though it must rest mainly on their own authority, which is however very great; Calvin keeps to the received sense and presses the deliberateness of the act

How the Angel is shown to be Christ: Gill argues from the works predicated, that the deliverance meant includes redemption from the guilt and punishment of sin and from everlasting wrath, which none but a divine Person could do; Clarke argues from the word Goel, which the law applies to the nearest kinsman whose right it is to redeem a forfeited inheritance, so that only he who took our flesh can bear it; Calvin argues from the worship, that Jacob so joins the Angel to God as to make him his equal, which would be absurd of a creature; Wesley simply asserts it

What the laying on of hands is: Keil defines it as a symbolical sign by which the one acting transferred to another a spiritual good, a supersensual power or gift, and both he and Clarke note that it appears here for the first time in Scripture and list the same later uses, while Clarke turns instead to the pattern of the younger preferred before the elder and resolves it into the secret counsel of God
outliers: Clarke's list of the reversals, Abel before Cain, Shem before Japheth, Isaac before Ishmael, Jacob before Esau, Judah and Joseph before Reuben, Ephraim before Manasseh, Moses before Aaron and David before his brethren

Calvin's inference from the deliberateness of the crossing, that a man too dim-sighted to distinguish the boys nevertheless crossed his hands on purpose, so that the Holy Spirit made him see more correctly than the clear-sighted

Clarke's note on the order of blessing, that the father is blessed first and the sons afterwards, which he takes for further proof of Jacob's superiority since the less is always blessed of the greater
Wesley's turn upon the clause about feeding, that we have never wanted food convenient and that he who has fed us all our life long will not fail us at last

Calvin's rule for the ministry drawn from Jacob's resort to prayer, that pastors entrusted with the dispensation of spiritual gifts are nothing compared with God and must keep their own place lest they obscure his name
Gill's insistence that Jacob would never have asked a created angel for blessings temporal and spiritual which a creature cannot give

17.pericope_label: Joseph would remove his father’s hand; the younger shall be greater; behold, I die
debates: How the prophecy of Ephraim’s greatness was fulfilled, where the two witnesses part company and neither notices the other: Ellicott reports that at the final numbering on the plains of Moab Manasseh had fifty-two thousand seven hundred and Ephraim only thirty-two thousand five hundred, so that on the figures the greatness went the wrong way, and explains it by the division of Manasseh, by Joshua being an Ephraimite and by the ark being placed in one of its towns; Wesley draws the opposite picture from a different census, that when the tribes were mustered in the wilderness Ephraim was the more numerous and had the standard of that squadron

Why Joseph objected: Clarke makes it natural affection working on a universal convention, that the right hand was reckoned the nobler and the instrument of conveying the highest dignities, and summarises that Joseph spoke as moved by natural affection while Jacob acted as influenced by the Holy Spirit; Calvin refuses to put the objection down to partiality at all, holding that it arose from faith and from holy reverence for the prophetic office, since Joseph would easily have borne the same thing had it been his father’s own doing rather than a prophet’s

What the composure at the announcement of death shows: Clarke builds an argument on it, that men could not act as the patriarchs did in their last moments if they had no hope of eternal life and no belief in the immortality of the soul; Calvin takes the same words as instruction rather than evidence, that Jacob mentions his death to teach that the eternal truth of God does not depend on the life of men; Wesley makes it pastoral, that the assurance was preserved so they might neither love Egypt too much when it favoured them nor fear it too much when it frowned
outliers: Clarke's admission that the reason for the universal precedence of the right hand is not particularly obvious, alongside his observation that even in the heavens the right hand of God is the place of most exalted dignity
Ellicott's comparison of Joshua after the conquest to General Washington after the independence of the United States had been secured, all Israel regarding him as their ruler and chief
Calvin's warning against those who hew out dry and perforated cisterns in seeking causes of divine adoption, since the primary source of election is God's free good pleasure
Wesley's arrival at nearly the same place from the other direction, that God often gives most to those who are least likely, choosing the weak things of the world and raising the poor out of the dust
Clarke's record that Jewish women say to their daughters at marriage, God make thee as Sarah and Rebekah, the forms being still in use

Calvin's account of why the promise is repeated, that no vision had appeared to Joseph's sons, so the holy old man, ordained as sponsor of the covenant, took timely precaution that their faith should not be shaken by his death

22.pericope_label: One portion above thy brethren, taken with my sword and with my bow
debates: Whether one Shechem names the town or describes a ridge: Gill reports that the Targum of Jonathan and Jarchi take it for the city and holds that the city is referred to though not directly meant; Calvin has no doubt a definite territory is meant and thinks the question closed by the evangelist and by the last chapter of Joshua; Ellicott alone argues both sides, setting against the town the objection that one Shechem is an unnatural way of describing a town and the lexical point that the word also means the shoulder and was given by Hebrews and Arabs alike to any elevated strip of ground, and resolving it as a play upon words intended to show that the town was really signified

How the taking by sword and bow squares with the purchase: Wesley supplies a history, that Jacob bought the land, was dispossessed by the Amorites and retook it by force; Calvin argues from the price that only a tent-place was bought and that the gift now takes in the much larger common land of the city; Ellicott addresses the other half of the phrase, that Shechem was strictly a Hivite town but that the name Amorite may have been used loosely, or to give the exploit greater glory; Gill denies the premises outright, that the place was taken neither from the Amorite nor by sword and bow

Whether the sack of the city by Simeon and Levi is meant: Gill refuses it on the ground that Jacob would never make his own act a deed he so abhorred and still abhorred in the chapter following; Ellicott refuses it on the ground that a man who condemns that exploit so strongly can scarcely be claiming it; Calvin rules out a different candidate, calling the interpretation that sword and bow stand figuratively for prayer and supplication still more improbable
outliers: Ellicott's citation of Abul-walid that the word also means the shoulder and that both Hebrews and Arabs gave the name to any elevated strip of ground
Calvin's calculation from the hundred pieces of silver, that anyone may reckon from the price how small a parcel Jacob actually possessed before the destruction of the city

Clarke's refusal to conjecture, that many attempts to explain the verse have all hitherto been fruitless, that the words were no doubt perfectly well understood by Joseph and probably allude to some transaction not now on record, and that it is much safer to confess our ignorance than to hazard conjecture after conjecture
Calvin's rejection of the figurative reading, that to take the sword and bow for prayer and supplication is still more improbable than the rest

Wesley's note that the parcel was given to Ephraim as their right and the lot was never cast upon it, and that Joseph's bones were buried in it, which he suspects Jacob had as much in view as anything in the settlement
Wesley's closing sentence, that it may sometimes be both just and prudent to give some children portions above the rest, but a grave is what we can most count upon as our own in this earth
themes: with my sword and with my bow
